keyVerseText: Now there was a man of Benjamin, whose name was Kish, the son of Abiel, the son of Zeror, the son of Bechorath, the son of Aphiah, a Benjamite, a mighty man of power. a Benjamite: or, the son of a man of Jemini power: or, substance
rootMeaning: The root of אֲפִיחַ (ʼĂphîyach) is likely connected to the Hebrew root פּוּחַ (pûwach), which carries the sense of blowing, breathing, or puffing. This root implies an action of causing breath or wind to move, suggesting life, animation, or stirring. The name אֲפִיחַ thus can be understood as 'I will make to breathe' or 'breath-giver,' highlighting a dynamic, life-giving aspect beyond the mere label of a proper name.
usageInScripture: The word אֲפִיחַ occurs only once in Scripture, appearing as a proper name in 1 Samuel 9:1. It is consistently translated as 'of Aphiah,' indicating a lineage or ancestral connection. This singular occurrence as a personal name points to its function primarily as an identifier rather than a common noun, but its root meaning enriches the understanding of the character's heritage as connected to life and breath.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding אֲפִיחַ as 'I will make to breathe' invites reflection on God as the source of life and breath, a theme central to Scripture and Christian faith. This name, attached to an ancestor of Saul, reminds believers that even the lineage of Israel’s first king is rooted in the divine provision of life and vitality. It underscores the biblical truth that all human strength and power, as exemplified by the 'mighty man of power' in the key verse, ultimately derive from God's sustaining breath. This connection encourages trust in God's ongoing work to enliven and empower His people.
keyVerseReflection: In 1 Samuel 9:1, the mention of Aphiah as an ancestor of Kish situates Saul's family within a lineage marked by strength and divine life-giving. The phrase 'the son of Aphiah' not only identifies heritage but subtly points to the life-giving breath implied by the name. This enriches the understanding of Saul's background as one grounded in God's sustaining power, preparing the way for his role as Israel's first king.
